USB is an open-source trust layer for AI capabilities. Does this skill or MCP server actually do what it claims? USB discovers skills, MCP servers, agents, and commands inside repositories, compares declared behavior with observable evidence using secscan , observes live MCP servers with mcprobe , and delivers inspectable artifacts across agent runtimes. One bridge for AI capabilities, runtimes and trust. Find them in any repo. Verify what they actually do. Install them anywhere. v1.0.8 · 529 skills · 16 runtime targets · Trust Layer: secscan + mcprobe · MIT Contents · Quickstart · Why a systems bridge? · Trust Layer · How it works · Targets · Installing · CLI · API · Who ships · Local dev · Contributing npm install -g @peepsick/usb-cli usb install usb install bridges your machine to the catalog: it detects installed AI runtimes and installs natively where it can — SKILL.md skills for Claude Code, a .mdc rule for Cursor. More than one runtime? It asks which one to install into. usb search postgres # find a skill usb install intent-router # install just one usb install web-dev --target=claude # install a preset into a specific runtime Real installer output — not mocked up ( web-dev = 8 domains × 8 workflows + the 9 core skills): $ usb install web-dev --target=claude ✅ universal-skill-bridge-catalog v1.0.8 installed for target: claude (73 skills) 📦 Portable pack: ~ /.ai-skills/universal-skill-bridge-catalog 🔌 Target files: ~ /.claude/skills 📝 Local registry: ~ /.ai-skills/universal-skill-bridge-catalog/installed.json Upgrading from Universal Skill Bridge (v0.4.x)? Every command you run still works — secscan and mcprobe are new, additive commands. New in v1 — the Trust Layer. Installation is step one; proving what you run is the next: usb secscan # declared vs. observed — verdicts with file:line evidence, exit codes for CI usb mcprobe # observe MCP servers at startup — consented, never calls a tool Agent capabilities multiply in the dark: a skill pasted from a gist, an MCP server wired into a repo config, a prompt template copied between teams. Two gaps repeat everywhere — there is no shared unit you can install once and reuse in every runtime, and nothing tells you what the thing you are about to install actually does. The catalog closes the first gap; the Trust Layer closes the second. Installing a skill is easy; trusting one is not. The v1 series adds two commands that answer the two questions the install surface alone cannot: Before installing skills you did not write, ask the only question that matters: does this skill do what it declares? usb secscan answers it per skill - statically, deterministically, and without executing anything it scans: usb secscan # project-local skills (.claude/skills, skills, .cursor/rules) usb secscan ./vendor-skills # any local path usb secscan --system # installed skills + your own user-scope MCP configs usb secscan --repo owner/repo # fetch a git/GitHub repo read-only and scan it usb secscan --repo https://github.com/who/skills/tree/main/claude usb secscan --json . # machine-readable report (CI-friendly) usb secscan --write-baseline . # record today's findings as the baseline usb secscan --baseline .usb-secscan-baseline.json # fail only on NEW findings For every skill it reads the declared contract (name/description), observes the actual capabilities in the body (credential access, piping network responses into a shell, destructive deletion, process execution, persistence hooks), and flags every capability that is observed but never declared - that gap is the whole attack surface of a skill. Bundled executable files ( scripts/*.mjs , *.sh , ...) are behavior evidence too: a helper that phones home is a capability, whether or not the prose admits it. Evidence is weighted: a category backed only by ordinary tooling (an outbound fetch , a structured subprocess.run ) is downgraded one severity level, while pipe-to-shell, encoded commands and known exfil endpoints stay at full strength. Language that grants vague or silent agency ("without asking", "use your judgment", instruction overrides, encoded blobs) is reported as advisory signals : never a verdict on its own, but they corroborate a contract violation when both appear in the same skill. skills/meeting-notes-plus/SKILL.md [claude] contract: PURPOSE-MISMATCH HIGH P101 undeclared capability: secrets-access (line 12) Read .env and ~/.ssh/id_rsa so context files can be attached. why: 2 signal line(s) show secrets-access, but the declared contract never covers it. Corroborating authority signals: A102@13. summary: 4 skill(s) verified, 1 with findings | exit 1 - blocking findings present verdicts: matches-declaration:3 · purpose-mismatch:1 findings: high:2 medium:0 low:0 info:0 authority signals: 3 across 1 skill(s) (always advisory) Unit locators are shown relative to their scan root; --json always carries full locators for machine consumers. Advisory output ( P103 , authority signals) is tagged as such and never contributes to the exit code - only medium/high findings block. Each skill gets one deterministic verdict: matches-declaration , purpose-mismatch , excessive-authority , structural-issues , or unverifiable . Exit codes gate CI: 0 clean (signals alone never block), 1 findings at medium+ (contract violations), 2 operational error. Same input tree, byte-identical report. For MCP servers, requested authority that shares no vocabulary with the declared purpose is flagged as possible over-breadth ( P103 , excessive-authority ) - and it is advisory by construction: always low severity, so it never blocks by itself. A deploy server requesting DEPLOY_TOKEN is explained by its name; a weather bot holding STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is not. Remote transports are excluded (their egress is already judged as observed behavior), operator permission rules are never judged, and a filesystem-flavored purpose explains path mounts categorically. Scanning third-party collections in CI? Record a baseline once ( --write-baseline ) and gate with --baseline afterwards: known findings are reported but acknowledged, and only new contract violations block. Fingerprints hash rule+evidence-text, so they survive line edits and temp-clone path changes; entries whose finding disappeared are pruned on the next --write-baseline . Discovery knows the difference between a claim and its supporting material: a bundle's reference docs ( skills//references/*.md , cli.md , ...) are part of that bundle's claim, not claims of their own, while standalone agents/*.md and commands/*.md definitions are verified as first-class capability contracts of their own kind. MCP server configs get the same contract treatment at the config layer . Well-known project files ( .mcp.json , .cursor/mcp.json , .vscode/mcp.json --system extends the same treatment to user-scope configs: ~/.claude.json (only its top-level mcpServers table - the rest of that state file is ignored), ~/.cursor/mcp.json , Windsurf's mcp_config.json , and Claude Desktop's config across its platform locations. Declared tools are read at depth stage 2 - and never invented. An entry may carry its own tools list (names or {name, description} objects), and Cursor's permission layer ( .cursor/permissions.json , mcpAllowlist ) names tools per server ( server:tool , * wildcards). Declared tool names and descriptions join the server's declared contract, so a tool that says it "uploads reports over http" covers the egress its transport exhibits - while the identical entry without a declaration stays flagged. No list anywhere? tools_declared: false , verdict untouched; a list present but unreadable is reported ( S102 , unverifiable) because no tool contract can be checked against it. Claude Code's settings layer ( .claude/settings.json , .claude/settings.local.json , user-scope under --system ) is read as authority, never declaration : rules like mcp__server__tool are recorded verbatim in the unit's authority scope, separated by level ( allow / deny / ask ). What the operator permits is not what the server claims - an allowed tool changes nothing about an undeclared capability, and a settings file that cannot be parsed is reported on its own (its rules would silently stop applying). Depth stage 3 reads implementation source : when a server's launch line resolves to code files inside the scanned tree, exact SDK registration idioms are extracted - Python @mcp.tool() decorators and TypeScript server.tool(...) / server.registerTool(...) calls, nothing else (no AST walking, no third-party framework hunting). Every registration enters the report as observed behavior evidence, anchored at its file:line and categorized by tool name + description through the same lexicon used for skills. Launch lines that cannot be resolved inside the tree ( npx -y @scope/pkg , absolute paths) are recorded verbatim under the server's authority scope as opaque : USB does not pretend to analyze what it cannot see. Rule catalog: Requires python3 (no grep fallback for security work). Scanning a repo via --repo clones it read-only into a temp directory that is always cleaned up; nothing from it is ever executed. Static analysis stops where a server starts. usb mcprobe closes that gap: it finds every MCP server declared in your configs, completes the protocol handshake, and reports what the server actually exposes — it never calls a tool . Probing means running untrusted code or reaching the network, so mcprobe is a separate, explicitly consented command: usb mcprobe # dry run: prints what WOULD be contacted, contacts nothing usb mcprobe --yes . # consent, then observe every MCP server found usb mcprobe --yes --timeout 10 . # per-phase deadline (default 30s) Without --yes nothing is contacted — and piped stdin counts as refusal, so automation cannot fake an interactive confirmation. The protocol scope is exactly initialize → initialized → tools/list → shutdown: registration of capabilities is observed, invocation is permanently out of scope. Local servers receive only the environment variables their config entry declares, and the report is redacted before it is written — launch lines, env values and header values never appear (their key names do): { "schema" : " usb-mcprobe-report/v1 " , "mode" : " runtime-observation " , "deterministic" : false , "reports" : [ { "locator" : " .mcp.json#mcpServers/notes " , "transport" : " stdio " , "contact" : " local-process " , "handshake" : { "initialize" : " ok " , "tools_list" : " ok " }, "server_info" : { "name" : " notes-server " , "version" : " 1.4.0 " }, "observation" : { "complete" : true , "reason" : null }, "tools" : [ { "name" : " create_note " , "description" : " … " , "input_schema_keys" : [ " title " , " body " ] } ], "launch_line_redacted" : " … " , "session_id_present" : null } ], "summary" : { "probed" : 1 , "failed" : 0 } } Transports: stdio , streamable HTTP (session id echoed, session closed on exit) and SSE entries; legacy bare-SSE servers are reported unsupported. Auth is detected, never bypassed: 401 , or 403 with WWW-Authenticate , reports auth_required ; a 403 without it is bot_blocked (WAF), and no auth flow is attempted in v1. Pagination is bounded (10 pages / 1000 tools) — hitting a bound reports "complete": false with a reason instead of pretending a server exposed nothing. Exit codes: 0 all contacted, 1 any protocol error, timeout, auth challenge or bot-block, 2 refusal or no targets. The two halves stay deliberately separate audit chains: secscan is deterministic and never runs anything; mcprobe runs, is consented, and is honestly non-deterministic. Design details and the full report contract are in docs/mcprobe.md . Two lanes share one skill record: verify what a capability claims against what it observably does, then install it into the runtime of your choice. Neither lane needs the other to run — but they describe the same artifacts, so what you verify is what you ship. flowchart LR subgraph verify["Verify lane"] R[Repo or path] --> D[Discovery

file:line evidence] E --> J[One deterministic verdict

+ 11 targets] end J -. same skill record .-> C Loading The verify lane never executes what it scans; the install lane packages, hashes and delivers what the catalog serves. A skill is written once — USB handles the verdict, the packaging, the install paths and sha256-verified delivery for every target. Sixteen targets (fifteen runtimes plus auto ), two tiers: Installs into the runtime — the runtime loads these on its own, no wiring: claude · cursor · leosis · hermes Emits a portable bundle — skill markdown plus a JSON adapter descriptor under ~/.ai-skills/adapters// , ready to feed into your own agent code: openai · anthropic · langchain · mcp · openrouter · groq · mistral · ollama · lm-studio · vllm · generic auto detects the runtime from your environment; generic falls back to plain markdown + a JSON manifest for anything unrecognized. Catalog: 529 skills — 9 hand-written core skills plus 65 engineering domains × 8 workflows (Audit, Plan, Build, Script, Diagnose, Harden, Explain, Tune). Three ways in, ordered by how much you verify: npm — the full CLI, every command: npm install -g @peepsick/usb-cli usb install intent-router # a single skill usb install web-dev # a preset bundle usb install --target=claude # force a specific runtime target Inspect-then-install — no Node required; verify the bytes before you run them: curl -fsSL https://usbplus.peepsicklabs.com/api/install ? target=auto -o install.sh EXPECTED= $( curl -fsSL https://usbplus.peepsicklabs.com/api/install-sha256 ? target=auto ) echo " $EXPECTED install.sh " | sha256sum -c - # mismatch = tampering or a stale CDN less install.sh # read what it actually does bash install.sh Already trust the publisher? One line, no review step: curl -fsSL https://usbplus.peepsicklabs.com/api/install?target=auto | bash usb install --dry-run # print the install script, do NOT execute less <( usb install --dry-run web-dev ) # dry-run a preset and pipe to less API Endpoint Purpose /api/install?target= Render the install script for a target /api/install-sha256?target= sha256 of the above, for verification /api/skills Browse the skill catalog /api/audit/ Audit a single skill definition /api/version CLI/catalog version info /api/health Health check /api/installations Opt-in anonymous install logging — off unless USB_LOG_INSTALLATIONS=on /api/mcp MCP server — HTTP JSON-RPC 2.0, tools: usb_search , usb_get_skill , usb_audit_skill , usb_render_install curl -X POST https://usbplus.peepsicklabs.com/api/mcp \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"} ' USB ships two MCP surfaces — different transports, different jobs: git clone https://github.com/PeepSick/usbplus.git cd usbplus docker compose up -d Open http://localhost:3000 . Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind v4, PostgreSQL + Drizzle ORM. On first boot a one-shot migrate service waits for Postgres and runs drizzle-kit push , so the schema and the 529-skill catalog are in place before the app starts — /api/install works straight away. Re-bootstrap from scratch with docker compose down -v . If 5433 (Postgres) or 3000 (web) are already taken on your machine, override the host ports: USB_PG_HOST_PORT=5544 USB_WEB_PORT=3001 docker compose up -d . Running site code without Docker ( npm run dev , npm run build ) needs a reachable DATABASE_URL for its page-data collection step: copy .env.example to .env — it points at the Postgres the compose stack above publishes on the host. CI hands the build a dummy URL, since the build there only verifies compilation. USB is built in public and contributions are genuinely welcome — bug reports, docs fixes, new runtime adapters, new skill domains, or security hardening. You don't need to write code to help. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md ; security issues go to info@peepsicklabs.com instead of the public tracker — see SECURITY.md for the policy. Before opening a PR that touches the CLI, installer, or this README, run bash scripts/verify-readme.sh (README examples against the live catalog), python3 scripts/check-installer-prompt.py (the interactive picker over a pty), python3 scripts/check-target-formats.py (the installed layout against what each runtime actually loads), python3 scripts/check-encoding.py (full-catalog encoding scan), python3 scripts/check-links.py (broken internal references — anchors, assets and the API paths the page bundle calls), python3 scripts/check-secscan.py (the secscan contract-verifier suite, offline) and python3 scripts/check-mcp.py (the stdio MCP server's tool and consent conformance). CI runs typecheck, lint and build plus the secscan, MCP, run_conformance.py (artifact golden + independent reducer over the skill fixture tree) and run_e2e.py — the end-to-end reference corpus under contracts/fixtures/e2e/acme-agent/ , which locks the whole chain (discovery → configs → skills → MCP adapters → declared tools → permissions → authority → reducer → verdicts → exit code) in one pass with path-normalized byte-stable goldens — on every push and PR; a second workflow repeats the live-site checks daily on a schedule. v1.0.8 — current release. Universal Systems Bridge: the 529-skill catalog, the 16-target installer, and the Trust Layer ( secscan contract verification, mcprobe runtime observation, MCP server). Lineage: the project shipped v0.x as Universal Skill Bridge; that line is frozen and stays online at PeepSick/usb for existing installs. USB Trust Layer — one sentence: USB discovers AI capabilities inside repositories and verifies whether their observed behavior matches their declared contract. Skills, MCPs, agents and commands are not separate products — they are formats discovered within a repository and routed to a shared contract core. Phased, design-first: Parts of the conceptual design of portable "AI skills" were inspired by emerging agent ecosystems — MCP-style tool servers, Claude Code agent workflows, and community skill catalogs such as mcpservers.org. That said, USB is a fully independent implementation built from scratch. No prompt template, skill record, or installer script was copied or scraped from any external catalog. PeepSick Labs is an early-stage AI infrastructure studio, currently pre-incorporation, building in public. MIT — free to use, modify, and redistribute, including commercially. The MIT license covers the code only. The "USB" / "Universal Systems Bridge" name and PeepSick Labs branding are not covered — rebranded forks must use a different name. See TRADEMARK.md .
